# Deployment

## Project Site (GitHub Pages)

The static site in `website/` is published to
**[https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/)**
by [`.github/workflows/pages.yml`](../.github/workflows/pages.yml).

- A push to `main` runs the website tests, builds `_site` from `website/`, and
  deploys the artifact with `actions/deploy-pages`.
- `workflow_dispatch` republishes the site from the Actions tab without a code
  change.
- Pages is configured with the "GitHub Actions" source, so there is no
  `gh-pages` branch. Removing `pages.yml` stops all publishing and the site
  returns 404.
- The `github-pages` environment only allows deployments from `main`.

## Hosted MCP Server

The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**,
Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents.

## Test Chat (UI)

Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser:

> **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)**

## MCP Server Endpoint

Integrate via the MCP protocol at:

> **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach
> out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a
> client.

## Hosted Studio

The Living Studio SPA is deployed to Cloudflare Workers:

| Environment | URL |
|---|---|
| Production (`main`) | **[https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/](https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/)** |
| Pull request preview | Posted automatically by Cloudflare Workers Builds as a PR comment |

Production deploys on every push to `main`. The Worker is `agentic-odi`; keep
`name` in `wrangler.jsonc` aligned with the Worker connected in the dashboard.
Preview builds run for non-production branches and are ephemeral: the Cloudflare
PR comment is the source of truth, so do not copy a preview URL into docs. The
hosted UI loads without a backend; canvas data, chat, and mutations need the
sidecar tunnel described below.

## Living Studio on a Free Cloudflare Worker

Workers Containers — the only way to run the Python sidecar entirely on
Cloudflare — requires the Workers Paid plan. On the free plan, the Worker serves
the built SPA as Workers Static Assets and proxies `/api/*` to the sidecar
through a free, account-less
[Cloudflare Quick Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/tunnel/get-started/quick-tunnels/).

`wrangler.jsonc` publishes `apps/studio/dist` with SPA fallback and runs the Worker
first for `/api/*`; `infra/cloudflare/worker.ts` forwards those calls to the
`SIDECAR_URL` secret. The browser only talks to the Worker origin, so the
sidecar's CORS list is not involved.

```bash
# 1. Build the SPA that the Worker uploads as static assets
npm --prefix apps/studio ci
npm --prefix apps/studio run build

# 2. Terminal A — MCP server (:8000) + sidecar (:8100)
python scripts/dev.py

# 3. Terminal B — free public URL for the sidecar (no account required)
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8100
# copy the https://<random>.trycloudflare.com URL it prints

# 4. Store the URL on the Worker, then deploy
npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL   # paste the trycloudflare URL
npx wrangler deploy
```

Workers Builds settings (Workers & Pages → your Worker → Settings → Builds):

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Production branch | `main` |
| Root directory | `/` |
| Build command | `npm --prefix apps/studio ci && npm --prefix apps/studio run build` |
| Deploy command | `npx wrangler deploy` |
| Preview command | `npx wrangler preview` |

A Worker has no run command: the Worker script runs on Cloudflare. Set `name` in
`wrangler.jsonc` to the Worker you created before the first deploy.

### Pull request previews

Workers Builds posts the build status and Preview URL to the pull request
automatically. To enable it:

1. Open the Worker → **Settings** → **Build** → **Branch control**.
2. Keep the production branch set to `main` and enable **Preview Builds**.
3. If Cloudflare shows **Set up Worker Previews**, complete the one-time switch.
   This cannot be reversed.
4. Confirm the Preview command is `npx wrangler preview`.

`wrangler.jsonc` must keep a `previews` block, even an empty one: the
`wrangler preview` command fails the build with "Your Wrangler configuration is
missing a `previews` block" without it. Assets and compatibility settings stay
at the top level, so `"previews": {}` is enough while Previews need no extra
settings. If a future Preview needs vars or bindings, add them under `previews`
with Preview-safe values.

Previews do not inherit production settings. The SPA loads from a Preview, but
`/api/*` returns `502 SIDECAR_URL is not configured` until a preview-specific
`SIDECAR_URL` secret is configured:

```bash
npx wrangler preview secret put SIDECAR_URL --name <branch>
```

When `--name` is omitted it defaults to the current git branch. Previews are
ephemeral, and pull requests from forks may not receive one. If Cloudflare does
not comment, paste the URL into the PR's **Deployment** section.

The `cf` CLI can inspect build triggers and recent builds (`cf builds triggers
list`, `cf builds list`) and create a Preview (`cf previews deploy`), but it does
not post GitHub PR comments. The Workers Builds Git integration owns the PR link;
`cf` is only an optional verification tool and requires `cf auth login`.

> [!NOTE]
> The sidecar runs on your machine, so the Worker only works while
> `python scripts/dev.py` and the Quick Tunnel are running. Quick Tunnel URLs
> change on every restart — update the secret with
> `npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL`. Chat also needs a reachable
> OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the Studio's **Settings**; the canvas, job map,
> and impact simulation work without one.

display.text:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Run Ruff Lint (no auto-fix)
        run: uv run ruff check .

      - name: Verify Ruff Formatting (no auto-fix)
        run: uv run ruff format --check .

  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Run Mypy
        run: uv run mypy apps packages

      - name: Run Mypy (website)
        run: uv run --directory website mypy .

  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Run Bandit
        run: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages

      - name: Run Bandit (website)
        run: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r website/

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}

      - name: Pytest
        run: |
          uv run pytest \
            --cov=agentic_odi_cli \
            --cov=agentic_odi_connectors \
            --cov=agentic_odi_core \
            --cov=agentic_odi_mcp_server \
            --cov=agentic_odi_studio_api \
            --cov-report=term-missing \
            --cov-report=xml:coverage.xml

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: coverage.xml
          if-no-files-found: error

      # One upload per run is enough; the 3.12 report is the canonical one.
      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        if: ${{ matrix.python-version == '3.12' }}
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v7
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          files: coverage.xml
          fail_ci_if_error: false

  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, typecheck, security, test]
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: CLI reports a version
        run: |
          version="$(uv run python -m agentic_odi_cli --version)"
          [ -n "$version" ]
          echo "OK: $version"

      - name: CLI exposes connectors commands
        run: |
          help="$(uv run python -m agentic_odi_cli connectors --help)"
          echo "$help" | grep -q list
          echo "$help" | grep -q ingest
          echo "OK: connectors help"

      - name: Installer installs from a simulated release
        run: bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh

      - name: MCP server boots and serves /mcp
        run: |
          uv run python -m agentic_odi_mcp_server > /tmp/mcp_server.log 2>&1 &
          SERVER_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -sfX POST http://localhost:8000/mcp \
              -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
              -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1,"params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"ci","version":"1"}}}' \
              -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          kill "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          wait "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "MCP server did not respond on :8000/mcp"
            cat /tmp/mcp_server.log
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "OK: MCP server responded with 200"

      - name: Living Studio sidecar serves the studio API
        run: |
          AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND=mcp uv run python -m agentic_odi_studio_api.main > /tmp/sidecar.log 2>&1 &
          SIDECAR_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8100/api/health/mcp \
              -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
              -d '{"mcp_url":"http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"}' -o /dev/null &&
              curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:8100/api/canvas?mcp_url=http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp" -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          kill "$SIDECAR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          wait "$SIDECAR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "Living Studio sidecar did not respond on :8100"
            cat /tmp/sidecar.log
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "OK: sidecar studio API responded with 200"

      - name: scripts/dev.py brings up both services and stops cleanly
        run: |
          uv run python scripts/dev.py > /tmp/clientrun.log 2>&1 &
          RUN_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -sf -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8100/api/config &&
              curl -sfX POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp \
                -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
                -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1,"params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"ci","version":"1"}}}' \
                -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "scripts/dev.py did not bring up both services"
            cat /tmp/clientrun.log
            kill "$RUN_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
            exit 1
          fi
          kill -INT "$RUN_PID"
          wait "$RUN_PID"
          echo "OK: both services stopped cleanly"

  website:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Pytest (website)
        run: uv run --directory website pytest tests/

      - name: Build site (rsync)
        run: |
          mkdir -p _site
          rsync -av website/ _site/ --exclude='tests/' --exclude='tools/'

  studio:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
        working-directory: apps/studio
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: "lts/*"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: apps/studio/package-lock.json

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Typecheck
        run: npm run typecheck

      - name: Unit tests
        run: npm test -- --run

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      - name: Verify generated API types are up to date
        run: |
          npm run gen:api-types
          git diff --exit-code -- src/api/schema.d.ts

  tauri-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
        working-directory: apps/studio/src-tauri
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install Linux webview dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential curl wget file \
            libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy

      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: apps/studio/src-tauri -> target

      - name: Cargo fmt
        run: cargo fmt --check

      - name: Cargo clippy
        run: cargo clippy -- -D warnings

      - name: Cargo check
        run: cargo check

  tauri-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install Linux webview dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential curl wget file \
            libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: "lts/*"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: apps/studio/package-lock.json

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: apps/studio/src-tauri -> target

      - name: Install frontend dependencies
        run: npm ci
        working-directory: apps/studio

      # Dependabot PRs cannot read repository secrets, so the signing key is
      # empty there. Export it only when present and disable updater artifacts
      # otherwise; passing an empty key makes the bundler try (and fail) to
      # decode it.
      - name: Build desktop bundle
        working-directory: apps/studio
        env:
          SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          SIGNING_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$SIGNING_KEY" ]; then
            export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$SIGNING_KEY"
            export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="$SIGNING_KEY_PASSWORD"
            npm run tauri -- build
          else
            echo "No TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY provided — building without signed updater artifacts."
            npm run tauri -- build --config '{"bundle":{"createUpdaterArtifacts":false}}'
          fi

      - name: Upload desktop bundles
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: tauri-bundles-linux
          if-no-files-found: warn
          path: |
            apps/studio/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/*.deb
            apps/studio/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/appimage/*.AppImage
            apps/studio/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/appimage/*.AppImage.sig

  ci-green:
    name: CI green
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, typecheck, security, test, smoke, website, studio, tauri-check, tauri-build]
    if: always()
    steps:
      - name: Verify all required jobs succeeded
        run: |
          results='${{ join(needs.*.result, ' ') }}'
          echo "Job results: $results"
          for result in $results; do
            if [ "$result" != "success" ]; then
              echo "::error::A required job did not succeed ($results)"
              exit 1
            fi
          done
          echo "OK: all required jobs succeeded"

parts.text:
Now, understanding the deployment: the studio-api is a *local sidecar* — it runs on the user's machine. The Cloudflare Worker only serves the SPA and proxies /api/* to a local sidecar through a Quick Tunnel. So "deploy" for the studio-api means... running it locally. Hmm.

Wait — the user said "we haven't still merged or deploy the code". So the plan is: merge the code (commit + PR to main?) and deploy (which for the sidecar means running it; and for the Worker means pushing to main triggers the Cloudflare build).

But the key thing: PostHog events are emitted from the studio-api (backend). The wizard verification needs events arriving at the PostHog project. Since the API key is in `.env` locally, we could just run the studio-api locally with the .env and trigger events.

Let me now understand the wizard's verification mechanism. The posthog wizard (npx -y @posthog/wizard@latest) — it's a CLI that detects the framework, applies integration, and then verifies by sending a test event and checking the PostHog API for it. It typically asks the user to run the app and then checks for events.

Let's check the `.entire` directory and `.pi` — maybe there's a transcript of what the agent did.

Also there's the `docs/superpowers/` dir mentioned in AGENTS.md. Let me check if there are existing plans/specs relating to posthog.

Let me check what state the repo is in and look for a plan.

1: # Agentic ODI - AI Developer Guardrails
2: 
3: This file provides system instructions and guardrails for any AI agents (or LLMs) assisting with the development of the **Agentic ODI** project. Please adhere to these guidelines to maintain consistency and align with the project's vision.
4: 
5: > **Source of Truth for ODI Methodology**: `docs/reference/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` by Anthony W. Ulwick (Strategyn). All ODI concepts in this project are grounded in that document. When in doubt, refer agents back to its definitions.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails
10: 
11: This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.
12: 
13: ### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?
14: 
15: ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.
16: 
17: ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done
22: 
23: - A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
24: - A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
25: - **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
26: - ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes
31: 
32: - **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
33: - Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
34: - **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):
35: 
36:   > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`
37: 
38:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
39:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
40:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
41:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.
42: 
43: - **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)
48: 
49: - All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
50:   1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
51:   2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
52:   3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
53:   4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
54:   5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
55:   6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
56:   7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
57:   8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs
58: 
59: - **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
60: - ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)
65: 
66: - Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
67:   - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
68:   - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?
69: 
70: - **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):
71: 
72:   ```
73:   Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
74:   ```
75: 
76: - **Interpretation**:
77:   - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
78:   - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
79:   - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.
80: 
81: - **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation
86: 
87: - ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
88: - Segments can be:
89:   - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
90:   - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
91:   - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value
92: 
93: - **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy
98: 
99: Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:
100: 
101: | Strategy | When to use |
102: |---|---|
103: | **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
104: | **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
105: | **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |
106: 
107: - **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent
112: 
113: These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:
114: 
115: | DO | DON'T |
116: |---|---|
117: | Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
118: | Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
119: | Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
120: | Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
121: | Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
122: | Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
123: | Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
128: - **Language**: Python 3.10+
129: - **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
130: - **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
131: - **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
132: - **UI / Chat Client**: React + Vite (`apps/studio`), FastAPI sidecar (`apps/studio-api`)
133: - **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
134: - **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
135: - **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail
140: 
141: `README.md` is the **primary human-facing entry point** for this project: a short,
142: high-level front door aimed at both users and developers. Detailed material lives
143: in `docs/` and is linked from the README. The agent MUST keep both current at all
144: times.
145: 
146: ### When to update
147: 
148: Update the relevant file whenever any of the following change:
149: 
150: | Change type | Where to update |
151: |---|---|
152: | New or removed Python file / package | `README.md` **Code Overview** |
153: | New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | `README.md` **Quick Start → Prerequisites** |
154: | New way to run the project | `README.md` **Quick Start** and `docs/living-studio.md` |
155: | New MCP tool or capability | `README.md` **Code Overview** / relevant doc |
156: | New CLI command or flag | `docs/cli.md` |
157: | New connector kind | `docs/connectors.md` |
158: | New workflow or agent instruction | `docs/living-studio.md` |
159: | Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | `docs/deployment.md` |
160: | Roadmap item completed or added | `docs/roadmap.md` |
161: | Test layout or coverage changes | `docs/development.md` |
162: 
163: ### Rules
164: 
165: - ✅ **Update docs in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
166: - ✅ **Keep README short**: it stays a high-level orientation page. Push detail into `docs/` and link to it rather than growing the README.
167: - ✅ **Keep the Quick Start accurate**: always reflect `uv run python scripts/dev.py` as the recommended launch command.
168: - ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
169: - ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
170: - ❌ **Never leave the README or `docs/` in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.
171: 
172: ---
173: 
174: ## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails
175: 
176: ### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
177: - **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
178: - **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
179:   - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
180:   - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
181: - **Tool Creation**: 
182:   - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
183:   - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
184:   - **Contract Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` (`ToolName`, `TOOL_SPECS`) and the `get_capabilities` return string. `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py` enforces the surface.
185: 
186: ### 2. Async / Client Practices
187: - Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
188: - Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.
189: 
190: ### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
191: - Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
192: - When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.
193: 
194: ### 4. General Philosophy
195: - **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
196: - **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
197: - **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `packages/connectors` workspace package. New kinds implement `agentic_odi_connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
198: - **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.
199: 
200: ### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
201: - **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
202: - **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
203: - **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `apps/mcp-server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `packages/connectors/src/agentic_odi_connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `packages/connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
204: - **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
205: - **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
206: - **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
207: - **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

(End of file - total 207 lines)

- ✅ **Update docs in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
- ✅ **Keep README short**: it stays a high-level orientation page. Push detail into `docs/` and link to it rather than growing the README.
- ✅ **Keep the Quick Start accurate**: always reflect `uv run python scripts/dev.py` as the recommended launch command.
- ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
- ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
- ❌ **Never leave the README or `docs/` in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.

---

## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails

### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
- **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
- **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
  - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
  - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
- **Tool Creation**: 
  - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
  - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
  - **Contract Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` (`ToolName`, `TOOL_SPECS`) and the `get_capabilities` return string. `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py` enforces the surface.

### 2. Async / Client Practices
- Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
- Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.

### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
- Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
- When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.

### 4. General Philosophy
- **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
- **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
- **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `packages/connectors` workspace package. New kinds implement `agentic_odi_connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
- **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.

### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
- **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
- **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
- **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `apps/mcp-server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `packages/connectors/src/agentic_odi_connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `packages/connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
- **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
- **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
- **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
- **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

# Local Dev & Test Workflow

Use this workflow whenever the user asks to:
- Run the app locally
- Test the agent/server/client stack end-to-end
- Open the browser and interact with the Living Studio SPA

## Steps

1. **Start the server** — Launch the FastMCP server and the Living Studio sidecar as a
   single background process using the dev launcher.

   ```
   uv run python scripts/dev.py
   ```

   Run with `WaitMsBeforeAsync: 2000` so the server has time to bind its port before
   continuing. Save the CommandId as `SERVER_CMD`.

2. **Verify the server is healthy** — Check `SERVER_CMD` status. If it has exited with an
   error, stop and report the error to the user. Do not proceed.

3. **Verify the studio is running** — Confirm the studio sidecar has started by checking
   for the "Living Studio" URL printout (`http://localhost:8100`).

4. **Open the browser** — Use the `browser_subagent` tool to navigate to
   `http://localhost:8100` and visually confirm the Living Studio SPA loads correctly.

5. **Run end-to-end interaction** — Use `browser_subagent` to exercise a feature
   (e.g., explore the Opportunity Landscape or query job maps) and confirm the UI
   responds correctly. Report what you see.

6. **Report results** — Use `notify_user` to summarize:
   - Whether the MCP server and studio sidecar started cleanly
   - What the browser showed
   - Any errors encountered

7. **Teardown (when done)** — Terminate `SERVER_CMD` using `send_command_input` with
   `Terminate: true`.

## Notes

- The MCP server runs on `http://localhost:8000/mcp`
- The Living Studio runs on `http://localhost:8100`
- All commands should be run from the project root (the `agentic-odi` workspace root).
- The MCP server does not require an LLM. The studio SPA is a static build; if the
  frontend is not built, the dev launcher prints a hint with the build command.

---README---

> have any feedback, please drop an email to **[wizard@posthog.com](mailto:wizard@posthog.com)**.

PostHog wizard ✨

The PostHog wizard helps you quickly add PostHog to your project using AI. ![Wizard clip](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmukukwp6/image/upload/q_auto,f_auto/pasted_image_2026_05_01_T19_53_26_002_Z_398f697f5c.png) # Usage To use the wizard, you can run it directly using: ```bash npx @posthog/wizard@latest ``` Currently the wizard can be used for over 16+ frameworks for frontend, backend, and mobile applications. If you have other integrations you would like the wizard to support, please open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/posthog/wizard/issues)! Visit our [docs](https://posthog.com/docs/ai-engineering/ai-wizard) to learn more. ## Privacy & data usage The wizard uses **AI models from Anthropic or OpenAI**, routed through PostHog's AI gateway, to read your project's source files and integrate PostHog. A few things worth knowing up front: - **Source files** are sent to the selected model provider as part of the agent's context. - **`.env*` files and secrets** stay on your machine. The wizard's security scanner blocks anything it identifies as a secret from being read by the agent. - **Telemetry** (run metadata — phase, task list, planned events) is sent to PostHog by default. Pass `--no-telemetry` (or set `POSTHOG_WIZARD_NO_TELEMETRY=1`) to disable. - **AI opt-in**: for existing organizations in interactive runs, the wizard checks `is_ai_data_processing_approved` and waits for approval before agent work. CI and signup runs bypass this interactive gate. - **Prefer your own AI?** The wizard's integration knowledge ships as a context-mill skill you can download and run inside your own agent. The wizard's "Privacy & data" menu (intro screen) and the `[I]` shortcut on the auth screen surface the same information in-terminal. ## MCP Commands The wizard also includes commands for managing PostHog MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers: ```bash # Install PostHog MCP server to supported clients npx @posthog/wizard@latest mcp add # Remove PostHog MCP server from supported clients npx @posthog/wizard@latest mcp remove # Try the PostHog MCP with your agent, no install needed npx @posthog/wizard@latest mcp tutorial ``` These, `slack`, `doctor`, `provision`, `cli add` and `skill list` are tools: commands that do their job without an agent run. See [src/tools](src/tools/README.md). ## Wizard programs The wizard's commands are grouped into **programs** — self-contained agentic jobs that install, audit, or wire up a specific piece of PostHog. They're powered by skills from the [context mill](https://github.com/PostHog/context-mill). ### PostHog integration (default) Running the wizard with no arguments installs PostHog into your project. It detects your framework, wires up initialization, instruments a starter set of events, and walks you through a first dashboard: ```bash npx @posthog/wizard@latest ``` Powered by the `posthog-integration` program. Most other programs below build on it and declare `requires: ['posthog-integration']`. ### Self-driving Autonomously sets up PostHog self-driving end-to-end. It connects GitHub, enables Session Replay and Error Tracking, wires up signal sources, and configures a Signals scout troop that watches your project for you. ```bash npx @posthog/wizard@latest self-driving ```

Hmm wait, but `git diff --name-status origin/main...HEAD` shows the three-dot diff (merge-base to HEAD) which includes the website redesign. So yes, the website files with lint errors are introduced by this branch.

Important consideration for "merge": the `posthog` branch carries the website redesign work too. Merging it to main will also merge the website redesign, which currently has lint failures. That's a problem for CI. Let me verify whether these lint errors would fail CI: CI runs `uv run ruff check .` at the root → yes, would fail with 6 errors. And `ruff format --check .` → 5 files would be reformatted → fails.

Hmm, wait. Are the website tests/tools excluded from ruff? `extend-exclude = [".agents/skills", ".worktrees", "docs/superpowers/plans"]` — website is not excluded. But CI has a separate "Ruff Lint (website)"? No — CI runs `uv run ruff check .` (whole repo) and `uv run --directory website mypy .`. So yes, root ruff covers website/.

So the branch has failing lint/format. That means merging to main as-is would break CI. Let me double-check by running ruff check on the merge-base state... Actually simpler: the failing files are all in website/ which only exist on this branch (new files added by the redesign). So they're new problems introduced by the branch.

This is a real blocker for the merge step and needs to be in the plan. But careful: is fixing website lint in scope? The user's objective is "complete the addition of posthog" — merge and deploy the code. If the branch has unrelated lint failures, CI blocks the merge. Options: (a) fix the 6 lint + 5 format issues (small, mechanical), (b) rebase the posthog commit onto main without the website work (split the branch).

Wait — actually, is the website redesign work *supposed* to be on this branch? The branch is named "posthog". The website redesign commits (037fc007, 898f4ba7, cb649020) plus plans/specs. Hmm, the branch was probably created for the website redesign and reused for posthog work. The user wants to "complete the addition of posthog" and "merge or deploy the code".

Let me now check origin/main's state: is the website redesign already in main? origin/main's last commits are 5286b6eb (Odi the Otter), 85478be5 (Intent-first Living Studio), 1eeb2e41 (docs specs). Let me check if website/ in origin/main has the redesign files.

`git diff --name-status origin/main...HEAD` shows A website/dist/... etc. — meaning those files exist in HEAD but not in origin/main. So the redesign is not in main.

Hmm, but hold on: `git diff origin/main...HEAD` is merge-base..HEAD. Let me directly check `git ls-tree origin/main website/`.

Gap analysis of the current PostHog work:

1. **mypy fails** (4 errors in router.py) — blocker.
2. **No tests** for the new PostHog code — CI coverage + repo convention (tests are "living documentation").
3. **No docs** — README (new dependency, env vars), docs/architecture, maybe a new `docs/posthog.md`? AGENTS.md requires README current.
4. **`.env.example`** is untracked — should be committed (it documents POSTHOG_API_KEY/POSTHOG_HOST). But wait: `.env` is at root and gitignored? Let me check .gitignore for `.env`. If `.env` is not ignored, we must not commit the real key. Let me check.
5. **`.claude/`** untracked — wizard-installed skill. Decide: commit or ignore.
6. **Personless events / no user identification** — the wizard pulled in `identify-users.md`. The current `_capture` doesn't pass a distinct_id. For a local single-user app, personless events are OK-ish, but the "correct" pattern per PostHog docs is to identify. The SPA could send `X-POSTHOG-DISTINCT-ID`. That may be over-engineering; I should ask the user.
7. **`debug` flag never true** — the `elif settings.debug: raise RuntimeError` branch is dead unless DEBUG=1 is set. Actually `debug: bool = False` in Settings means env var `DEBUG` (pydantic-settings maps field name `debug` → env `DEBUG` case-insensitive). So `DEBUG=1` enables it. Fine, but the error message is odd.
8. **Health check logs** — `posthog_log.info("Studio API health check completed")` on every health check could be noisy; the CI smoke test hits /health repeatedly. Each health check emits an OTel log record → exported to PostHog. That's noisy but intentional? It's the "logs" feature. Hmm, and `posthog_log` records go through the OTel BatchLogRecordProcessor → exported to `{host}/i/v1/logs`. Does PostHog's `/i/v1/logs` endpoint exist? PostHog supports OTLP logs ingestion at `/i/v1/logs`? Let me verify. PostHog docs: "Log capture" — PostHog supports OTLP logs via `https://us.i.posthog.com/i/v1/logs`. I believe yes, PostHog added log ingestion (Logs product) with OTLP support at `/i/v1/logs`. Let me verify via web fetch of posthog docs to be sure the endpoint and auth header are right.

Actually let me check the posthog-python SDK — it has a `logs` feature? Hmm, in posthog-python 7.x there's `posthog.capture_log`? Let me check the installed SDK for a logs API, since using the SDK's own log capture would be simpler than hand-rolled OTel.

Let me check the installed posthog package.

9. **The `capture_unhandled_exception` handler** — `@app.exception_handler(Exception)` with `raise exc` inside. In Starlette, the handler for `Exception` is used by `ServerErrorMiddleware`, which re-raises the exception after the handler returns to let the server log it. So the app returns a 500 via ServerErrorMiddleware's error response. This works but duplicates `enable_exception_autocapture=True` (the SDK's sys.excepthook may already capture). Minor.

10. **Missing: `.env` in deployment environments.** For the sidecar to emit events in "production", the key must be present. For the local dev machine, `.env` exists. For the hosted studio (workers.dev) the sidecar is the user's machine. So "deploy" = the user's local sidecar + the tunnel. Hmm.

# Logs

Canonical URL: https://posthog.com/docs/logs

Logs is an OpenTelemetry-native log store, so there are no PostHog-specific SDKs to adopt – point any OTLP client at PostHog and your log records start arriving. Search them by service, severity, and attribute, group similar lines into [patterns](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/patterns.md) to see what changed, and open any record to have [PostHog AI](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/explain-logs-ai.md) explain it.

Because your logs live next to the rest of your data, a log line is one click from the [session replay](https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay.md), [person](https://posthog.com/docs/data/persons.md), and [error](https://posthog.com/docs/error-tracking.md) it belongs to.

[Get started](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/start-here.md)

## Where you can use it

You search and investigate logs in the [web app](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/surfaces/web-app.md). The other surfaces are for pulling log context into the tools you already work in.

PostHog Web

Search and filter logs, mine patterns, save views, and set up alerts.

[Search your logs →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/surfaces/web-app.md)

PostHog MCP

Let your coding agent query logs, mine patterns, and manage alerts from your editor.

[Debug logs →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/surfaces/mcp.md)

API

Query logs and manage alerts, saved views, and sampling rules programmatically.

[Use the API →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/surfaces/api.md)

## Where its data comes from

Everything in Logs is derived from the log records you send over [OTLP](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/installation.md). How useful they are depends on what you attach to them.

Services

Every record carries a `service.name`, which is how logs are grouped, faceted, and alerted on.

[Send your first logs →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/installation.md)

Attributes

Log and resource attributes become the facets you filter on – and the fields PII scrubbing protects.

[Structure your logs →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/best-practices.md)

Session replay and persons

Add a session ID and distinct ID and each log line links to the replay and person behind it.

[Link your logs →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/link-session-replay.md)

Patterns

PostHog masks the variable parts of your messages and clusters them into templates you can diff over time.

[See log patterns →](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/patterns.md)

# Python Logs installation

Canonical URL: https://posthog.com/docs/logs/installation/python

> **Cloud region:** This page uses US Cloud hosts. For an EU Cloud project, use `https://eu.i.posthog.com` instead of `https://us.i.posthog.com` (ingestion host), and use `https://eu.posthog.com` instead of `https://app.posthog.com` (app host for links).

## On this page

- [Install OpenTelemetry packages](#install-opentelemetry-packages)
- [Get your project token](#get-your-project-token)
- [Configure the SDK](#configure-the-sdk)
- [Use OpenTelemetry logging](#use-opentelemetry-logging)
- [Test your setup](#test-your-setup)
- [Next steps](#next-steps)

1.  1

    ## Install OpenTelemetry packages

    Required

    ```bash
    pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
    ```

2.  2

    ## Get your project token

    Required

    You'll need your PostHog project token to authenticate log requests. This is the same key you use for capturing events and exceptions with the PostHog SDK.

    > **Important:** Use your **project token** which starts with `phc_`. Do **not** use a personal API key (which starts with `phx_`).

    You can find your project token in [Project Settings](https://app.posthog.com/settings).

3.  3

    ## Configure the SDK

    Required

    Set up the OpenTelemetry SDK to send logs to PostHog.

    > **Note:** The logs API is still experimental in `opentelemetry-python`, so it's only exposed under the private `_logs` import path (e.g. `opentelemetry._logs`). Use these imports rather than `opentelemetry.logs`, which doesn't exist yet.

    ```python
    import logging
    from opentelemetry._logs import set_logger_provider
    from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider, LoggingHandler
    from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import BatchLogRecordProcessor
    from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http._log_exporter import OTLPLogExporter
    
    # Configure the logger provider
    logger_provider = LoggerProvider()
    set_logger_provider(logger_provider)
    
    # Create OTLP exporter with API key in header
    otlp_exporter = OTLPLogExporter(
        endpoint="https://us.i.posthog.com/i/v1/logs",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer <ph_project_token>"}
    )
    
    # Add processor
    logger_provider.add_log_record_processor(
        BatchLogRecordProcessor(otlp_exporter)
    )
    
    # Attach the OpenTelemetry handler to the root logger
    logging.getLogger().addHandler(LoggingHandler(logger_provider=logger_provider))
    ```

    Alternatively, you can pass the API key as a query parameter:

    ```python
    otlp_exporter = OTLPLogExporter(
        endpoint="https://us.i.posthog.com/i/v1/logs?token=<ph_project_token>"
    )
    ```

4.  4

    ## Use OpenTelemetry logging

    Required

    With the handler attached in the previous step, you can start logging with standard Python logging and the records flow to PostHog:

    ```python
    import logging
    
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    
    # Use standard Python logging
    logger = logging.getLogger("my-app")
    logger.info("User action", extra={"userId": "123", "action": "login"})
    logger.warning("Deprecated API used", extra={"endpoint": "/old-api"})
    logger.error("Database connection failed", extra={"error": "Connection timeout"})
    ```

5.  5

    ## Test your setup

    Recommended

    Once everything is configured, test that logs are flowing into PostHog:

    1.  Send a test log from your application
    2.  Check the PostHog Logs interface for your log entries
    3.  Verify the logs appear in your project

    [View your logs in PostHog](https://app.posthog.com/logs)

7.  ## Next steps

    Checkpoint

    *What you can do with your logs*

    | Action | Description |
    | --- | --- |
    | **[Why you need logs](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/basics.md)** | What logs show you that nothing else does |
    | **[Search logs](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/search.md)** | Use the search interface to find specific log entries |
    | **Filter by level** | Filter by `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, etc. |
    | **[Link session replay](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/link-session-replay.md)** | Connect logs to users and session replays by passing `posthogDistinctId` and `sessionId` |
    | **[Link logs to a person](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/link-person.md)** | Surface every log emitted on behalf of a user on their PostHog person profile |
    | **[Logging best practices](https://posthog.com/docs/logs/best-practices.md)** | Learn what to log, how to structure logs, and patterns that make logs useful in production |

    ```bash
    pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
    ```

2.  2

    ## Get your project token

    Required

    You'll need your PostHog project token to authenticate log requests. This is the same key you use for capturing events and exceptions with the PostHog SDK.

    > **Important:** Use your **project token** which starts with `phc_`. Do **not** use a personal API key (which starts with `phx_`).

    You can find your project token in [Project Settings](https://app.posthog.com/settings).

3.  3

    ## Configure the SDK

    Required

    Set up the OpenTelemetry SDK to send logs to PostHog.

    > **Note:** The logs API is still experimental in `opentelemetry-python`, so it's only exposed under the private `_logs` import path (e.g. `opentelemetry._logs`). Use these imports rather than `opentelemetry.logs`, which doesn't exist yet.

    ```python
    import logging
    from opentelemetry._logs import set_logger_provider
    from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider, LoggingHandler
    from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import BatchLogRecordProcessor
    from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http._log_exporter import OTLPLogExporter
    
    # Configure the logger provider
    logger_provider = LoggerProvider()
    set_logger_provider(logger_provider)
    
    # Create OTLP exporter with API key in header
    otlp_exporter = OTLPLogExporter(
        endpoint="https://us.i.posthog.com/i/v1/logs",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer <ph_project_token>"}
    )
    
    # Add processor
    logger_provider.add_log_record_processor(
        BatchLogRecordProcessor(otlp_exporter)
    )
    
    # Attach the OpenTelemetry handler to the root logger
    logging.getLogger().addHandler(LoggingHandler(logger_provider=logger_provider))
    ```

    Alternatively, you can pass the API key as a query parameter:

    ```python
    otlp_exporter = OTLPLogExporter(
        endpoint="https://us.i.posthog.com/i/v1/logs?token=<ph_project_token>"
    )
    ```

4.  4

    ## Use OpenTelemetry logging

    Required

    With the handler attached in the previous step, you can start logging with standard Python logging and the records flow to PostHog:

    ```python
    import logging
    
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    
    # Use standard Python logging
    logger = logging.getLogger("my-app")
    logger.info("User action", extra={"userId": "123", "action": "login"})
    logger.warning("Deprecated API used", extra={"endpoint": "/old-api"})
    logger.error("Database connection failed", extra={"error": "Connection timeout"})
    ```

5.  5

    ## Test your setup

    Recommended

    Once everything is configured, test that logs are flowing into PostHog:

    1.  Send a test log from your application
    2.  Check the PostHog Logs interface for your log entries
    3.  Verify the logs appear in your project

    [View your logs in PostHog](https://app.posthog.com/logs)

7.  ## Next steps

Yes: without `with`, the lifespan does NOT run.

So currently, the tests would NOT trigger the lifespan → no PostHog client → no events. """
Local dev launcher for Agentic ODI.

Starts the FastMCP server (``python -m agentic_odi_mcp_server``) and the Living
Studio sidecar (``uvicorn agentic_odi_studio_api.app:create_app --factory``)
concurrently, then prints the MCP and Studio URLs. Shutting down this script
(Ctrl+C) terminates both processes.

Usage:
    uv run python scripts/dev.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import signal
import socket
import subprocess  # nosec B404 - launches only fixed child commands (see B603 notes)
import sys
import time

MCP_PORT = 8000
STUDIO_PORT = 8100

REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SPA_DIST = os.environ.get(
    "AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DIST", os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "apps", "studio", "dist")
)
SPA_BUILD_HINT = (
    "Frontend not built — run `npm --prefix apps/studio run build` to serve the Studio UI."
)


def is_port_in_use(port: int) -> bool:
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as s:
        return s.connect_ex(("localhost", port)) == 0


def build_commands() -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
    """Return the (mcp_server, sidecar) argv lists, both shell-free and fixed."""
    mcp_command = [sys.executable, "-m", "agentic_odi_mcp_server"]
    sidecar_command = [
        sys.executable,
        "-m",
        "uvicorn",
        "agentic_odi_studio_api.app:create_app",
        "--factory",
        "--host",
        "127.0.0.1",
        "--port",
        str(STUDIO_PORT),
    ]
    return mcp_command, sidecar_command


def start_server() -> subprocess.Popen:
    if is_port_in_use(MCP_PORT):
        print(f"Error: Port {MCP_PORT} is already in use.")
        print("Please stop any process running on this port and try again.")
        sys.exit(1)

    mcp_command, _ = build_commands()
    print(f"Starting MCP server on http://localhost:{MCP_PORT}/mcp ...")
    # Fixed command, no shell, no untrusted input.
    return subprocess.Popen(mcp_command)  # nosec B603


def start_studio() -> subprocess.Popen:
    if is_port_in_use(STUDIO_PORT):
        print(f"Warning: Port {STUDIO_PORT} is already in use. The sidecar may fail to start.")

    _, sidecar_command = build_commands()
    print(f"Starting Living Studio sidecar on http://localhost:{STUDIO_PORT} ...")
    # Fixed command, no shell, no untrusted input.
    return subprocess.Popen(sidecar_command)  # nosec B603


def main() -> None:
    server = None
    studio = None

=== ARCH README ===
# Repository Architecture

Agentic ODI is a uv workspace with a single root `pyproject.toml` for shared tooling. Python distributions are imported by their stable `agentic_odi_*` package names; directory layout does not leak into imports.

## Layout

```text
apps/
  cli/            agentic_odi_cli         Typer CLI: local SQLite or remote MCP
  mcp-server/     agentic_odi_mcp_server  FastMCP server over HTTP
  studio-api/     agentic_odi_studio_api  FastAPI sidecar for the Studio SPA
  studio/         React + TypeScript + Vite SPA and Tauri 2 shell
packages/
  core/           agentic_odi_core        Domain, services, repositories, contract
  connectors/     agentic_odi_connectors  MCP client connectors and catalog
infra/cloudflare/ Worker + Wrangler config for the free-plan deployment
scripts/          Dev launcher, binary build, installer checks
tests/            Cross-package contract and launcher tests only
docs/             Architecture, reference material, Superpowers artifacts
packaging/        PyInstaller spec for the CLI binary
```

## Dependency Direction

```text
apps/cli ──────────────┐
apps/mcp-server ───────┼──▶ packages/core
apps/studio-api ───────┘         ▲
                                 │
apps/cli ──────────────▶ packages/connectors
```

- `packages/core` depends on no other workspace package.
- `packages/connectors` depends on `core` only where it needs shared models.
- Every runnable app may depend on `core`; none of them imports another app.
- The React SPA only talks to `apps/studio-api` over `/api`; it never calls MCP or the LLM directly.

## Persistence

- `SQLiteRepository` is the production default for the CLI, MCP server, and Studio API.
- The default database is `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`, overridable with `AGENTIC_ODI_DB`.
- `build_repository()` chooses SQLite by default and `InMemoryRepository` when `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:`, which is what tests use.
- The CLI selects its backend with `--backend local|mcp` or `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND`.
- The Studio API selects `local` (direct service calls) or `mcp` (passthrough) with `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` or `create_app(backend=...)`.

## MCP Contract

`packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` owns `ToolName`, `ToolSpec`, `TOOL_SPECS`, and `TOOL_NAMES`. The live FastMCP registry is asserted against it by `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py`; the CLI's local handlers are checked by `tests/contract/test_cli_contract.py`.

## Entry Points

| Command | Module |
|---|---|
| `agentic-odi` | `agentic_odi_cli.cli:app` |
| `agentic-odi-server` / `agentic-odi-mcp-server` | `agentic_odi_mcp_server.mcp_server:main` |
| `agentic-odi-studio-api` | `agentic_odi_studio_api.main:main` |
| `uv run python scripts/dev.py` | Dev launcher (MCP + Studio API) |

Let me also double check one important runtime aspect: does `posthog.capture()` in the sync client work from within FastAPI's threadpool (the router handlers are sync `def` → run in a threadpool)? Yes, the SDK is thread-safe.

But `Posthog.capture()` with `sync_mode=False` (default) queues events in a background consumer. The `shutdown()` flushes. We call `posthog_client.shutdown()` in the lifespan teardown. Good.

One more: `atexit.register(posthog_client.shutdown)` — shutdown is called twice (atexit + lifespan). The second call should be harmless (SDK's shutdown is idempotent-ish). Minor.

Now let me also double-check the `app.py` `create_app` function: `lifespan` is defined at module level, referencing `get_settings()`. Fine.

Another potential issue: `Posthog(...)` is created with `enable_exception_autocapture=True` → the SDK installs a global excepthook. Combined with the FastAPI exception handler, exceptions might be captured twice. Also, with autocapture, the SDK captures *unhandled* exceptions in the main thread via `sys.excepthook` — which fires when the process crashes, not per-request. The FastAPI handler captures per-request. So both are useful, though there might be double-capture of the same exception if the server re-raises it at the top level (uvicorn logs it and the excepthook fires). Actually `ServerErrorMiddleware` re-raises the exception → uvicorn catches it → uvicorn's error handler logs it; uvicorn doesn't call `sys.excepthook` (it handles exceptions itself in `Server.handle_error`). PostHog has a powerful API that enables you to capture, evaluate, create, update, and delete nearly all of your information in PostHog. The API is available for all users and instances. It contains two types of endpoints:

1.  **Public POST-only endpoints** such as [`/i/v0/e`](https://posthog.com/docs/api/capture.md) and [`/flags`](https://posthog.com/docs/api/flags.md) are used for capturing events, batching events, updating person or group information, and evaluating feature flags. These don't require authentication, but use [your project token](https://app.posthog.com/project/settings) to handle the request.

2.  **Private `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` endpoints** are used for [querying](https://posthog.com/docs/api/queries.md), creating, updating, or deleting nearly all data in PostHog. They give the same access as if you were logged into your PostHog instance, but require authentication with your personal API key.

> You must make API requests to the correct domain. On US Cloud, these are `https://us.i.posthog.com` for public endpoints and `https://us.posthog.com` for private ones. On EU Cloud, these are `https://eu.i.posthog.com` for public endpoints and `https://eu.posthog.com` for private ones. For self-hosted instances, use your self-hosted domain. Confirm yours by checking your PostHog instance URL.

## Authentication

Private endpoints require authentication. There are three ways to authenticate, and which one you should use depends on who the integration is for:

-   **[Personal API keys](https://posthog.com/docs/api/personal-api-keys.md)** – Use these when you're using PostHog from your own scripts, automations, or any integration tied to your own account. This is the right choice if you're just building something for your own project.
-   **[Project secret API keys](https://posthog.com/docs/api/project-secret-api-keys.md)** (beta) – Use these for server-to-server access that isn't tied to a user, such as a backend service executing [Endpoints](https://posthog.com/docs/endpoints.md). They're scoped to a single project and only have the scopes you grant them. They're rolling out gradually, so they may not be available in your organization yet.
-   **[OAuth](https://posthog.com/docs/api/oauth.md)** – Use this when you're building an app that other PostHog users will install or connect to. OAuth lets users grant your app scoped access without sharing their personal API key.

## Rate limiting

Private `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` endpoints are rate limited. Public POST-only endpoints are **not** rate limited. A rule of thumb for whether rate limits apply is if the personal API key is used for authentication.

There are separate limits for different kinds of resources.

-   For all analytics endpoints (such as calculating insights, retrieving persons, or retrieving session recordings), the rate limits are `240/minute` and `1200/hour`.

-   For the `events/values` endpoint, the rate limits are `60/minute` and `300/hour`. When using a personal API key, the `event_name` query parameter is required. For queries without event filters, use the [`query`](https://posthog.com/docs/api/queries.md) endpoint instead.

-   The [`query`](https://posthog.com/docs/api/queries.md) endpoint has a rate limit of `2400/hour`. Queries made with a personal API key also draw from an [hourly read budget](https://posthog.com/docs/api/queries.md#hourly-read-budget). For regular exports of events, use [batch exports](https://posthog.com/docs/data-pipelines/batch-exports.md). For large one-off exports, use [file download exports](https://posthog.com/docs/data-pipelines/file-download-exports.md). For data-powered APIs or user-facing dashboards, [reach out to us](https://posthog.com/talk-to-a-human).

-   For [feature flag local evaluation](https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/local-evaluation.md) (which is enabled in SDKs when you input a personal API key), the rate limit is `600/minute`.

-   For [prompt](https://posthog.com/docs/prompt-management.md) fetches made with a personal API key (reading a prompt by name or listing prompts, as the SDKs do), the rate limit is `600/minute`. This limit is separate from the general API limits, so polling clients do not use up the budget for other endpoints.

-   For the rest of the create, read, update, and delete endpoints, the rate limits are `480/minute` and `4800/hour`.

-   For the `/invites` and `/invites/bulk` endpoints, you can send `50` invites per hour and `200` per day, with up to 20 invites per bulk request. This also applies to invites sent from the PostHog UI.

-   Public POST-only endpoints such as event capture (`/e`, `/i/v0/e`) and feature flag evaluation (`/flags`) have no request-level rate limits. Event capture still returns `200` when your project is over its billing quota, and names the limited resources in the `quota_limited` field of the response body. It also applies a [per-distinct-ID ingestion protection](https://posthog.com/docs/how-posthog-works/ingestion-pipeline.md#rate-limiting-high-volume-distinct-ids): if a single distinct ID sends a high, sustained volume of events (roughly 5,000 per minute), those events are still accepted with a `200` response but are processed without strict ordering and without person profile updates for the duration of the spike. PostHog logs an [ingestion warning](https://posthog.com/docs/data/ingestion-warnings.md) when this happens.

Most of these limits count **per personal API key**, not per team. For example, if a script using one personal API key hits the rate limit, another user calling the persons API with a different personal API key is unaffected.

Two things change this. Requests that authenticate another way, such as OAuth or a logged-in session in the PostHog app, do not count against these personal API key limits. Some endpoints also set their own limits that count per project or per organization, so everyone shares one budget no matter how many keys they use. The `/invites` limits above work this way: they count per organization, and include invites sent from the PostHog UI.

> At this time, we are not offering higher limits than these, but you may wish to try our [endpoints product](https://posthog.com/docs/endpoints.md), which offers query customization and higher limits. Alternatively, you may be able to use our [batch exports product](https://posthog.com/docs/data-pipelines/batch-exports.md) to pull the data that you need from our events or persons tables on a faster cadence, or a [file download export](https://posthog.com/docs/data-pipelines/file-download-exports.md) for a one-off export.

## Responses

### Status code: 200

**Response:**

```json
{
  "status": "Ok"
}
```

**Meaning:** A `200: OK` response means we have successfully received the payload, it is in the correct format, and the project token (`token`) is valid. It **does not** imply that events are valid and will be ingested. As mentioned in [invalid events](https://posthog.com/docs/api/capture.md#invalid-events), certain event validation errors may cause an event not to be ingested.

### Status code: 400

**Responses:**

```json
{
  "type": "validation_error",
  "code": "invalid_project",
  "detail": "Invalid Project ID.",
  "attr": "project_id"
}
```

**Meaning:** We were unable to determine the project to associate the events with.

```json
{
  "type": "validation_error",
  "code": "invalid_payload",
  "detail": "Malformed request data",
  "attr": null
}
```

**Meaning:** Request payload data formatted incorrectly.

### Status code: 401

**Responses:**

```json
{
  "type": "authentication_error",
  "code": "invalid_api_key",
  "detail": "Project token invalid. You can find your project token in your PostHog project settings."
}
```

**Meaning:** The project token you provided is invalid.

```json
{
  "type": "authentication_error",
  "code": "invalid_personal_api_key",
  "detail": "Invalid Personal API key."
}
```

**Meaning:** The personal API key you used for authentication is invalid.

### Status code: 503 (Deprecated)

**Response:**

```json
{
  "type": "server_error",
  "code": "fetch_team_fail",
  "detail": "Unable to fetch team from database."
}
```

**Meaning:** (Deprecated) This error only occurs in self-hosted Postgres instances if the database becomes unavailable. On ClickHouse-backed instances database failures cause events to be added to a dead letter queue, from which they can be recovered.

## Pagination

Requests are paginated if the results are higher than the limit, usually 100 (sometimes 500 or 1000). Pagination happens in the following format:

```json
{
  "next": "<ph_app_host>/api/person/?cursor=cD0yMjgxOTA2",
  "previous": null,
  "results": [
    // ...
  ]
}
```

You can then just call the `"next"` URL to get the next set of results.

## Tips

-   When logged in, you can view and download the API schema using the following options:

    -   [Download the OpenAPI spec](https://app.posthog.com/api/schema/)
    -   [View the API schema with Swagger UI](https://app.posthog.com/api/schema/swagger-ui/)
    -   [View the API schema with Redoc](https://app.posthog.com/api/schema/redoc/)
-   The [`/users/@me/` endpoint](https://posthog.com/docs/api/user.md) gives you useful information about the current user.

-   The `/api/event_definition/` and `/api/property_definition` endpoints provide the possible event names and properties you can use throughout the rest of the API.

-   The maximum size of a POST request body is governed by `settings.DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE`, and is 20MB by default.

-   By default, the PostHog API returns results from the last project you visited in the UI. To override this behavior, you can pass in your project token as a query parameter in the request like `api/event/?token=my_project_token`.

## GitHub secret scanning

PostHog partners with GitHub to automatically detect exposed API keys in public repositories. When GitHub detects a leaked key, we take immediate action:

-   **Personal API keys** (`phx_`): The key is automatically rolled and the user is notified via email.
-   **Project secret API keys** (`phs_`): The key is automatically rolled and project admins and owners are notified via email.
-   **Feature flags secure API keys** (legacy, also `phs_`): Project admins and owners are notified via email. To revoke a leaked key, rotate it and then delete the backup key, since the backup stays active.
-   **OAuth access tokens** (`pha_`): The key and its associated refresh token are automatically revoked and the user is notified via email.
-   **OAuth refresh tokens** (`phr_`): The key and its associated access token are automatically revoked and the user is notified via email.

This provides an automatic layer of protection, but you should still follow best practices: never commit API keys to version control, use environment variables, and rotate keys if you suspect exposure.

display.text:
"""Event-store contract shared by local SQLite and cloud adapters."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import uuid
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, Protocol, TypedDict

DEFAULT_WORKSPACE = "local"
DEFAULT_DEVICE = "local"


class Event(TypedDict):
    """A single append-only domain event."""

    id: int
    event_id: str
    workspace_id: str
    device_id: str
    timestamp: str
    type: str
    payload: dict[str, Any]
    server_seq: int | None


class EventStore(Protocol):
    """Persistence boundary for the append-only event log."""

    def append(
        self,
        event_type: str,
        payload: dict[str, Any],
        *,
        event_id: str | None = None,
        workspace_id: str = DEFAULT_WORKSPACE,
        device_id: str = DEFAULT_DEVICE,
    ) -> Event: ...

    def get_stream(
        self,
        *,
        workspace_id: str | None = None,
        after_server_seq: int = 0,
        unsynced_only: bool = False,
        replay_order: bool = False,
    ) -> list[Event]: ...

    def insert_remote(self, events: list[Event]) -> int: ...

    def mark_synced(self, server_seqs: dict[str, int]) -> int: ...

    def retag_workspace(self, old: str, new: str) -> int: ...

    def max_server_seq(self, workspace_id: str) -> int: ...

    def get_cursor(self, workspace_id: str) -> int: ...

    def set_cursor(self, workspace_id: str, remote_url: str, seq: int) -> None: ...

    def pending_count(self, workspace_id: str) -> int: ...

    def clear(self, *, workspace_id: str | None = None) -> None: ...

    def close(self) -> None: ...


def new_event_id() -> str:
    """Return a globally unique, client-generated event identifier."""
    return uuid.uuid4().hex


def default_device_path() -> Path:
    return Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.agentic-odi/device_id"))


def resolve_device_id(path: Path | None = None) -> str:
    """Return a stable random device id, creating it on first use.

    The id is deliberately random: it must not reveal a hostname, user, or
    anything else about the device.
    """
    configured = os.environ.get("AGENTIC_ODI_DEVICE_ID")
    if configured:
        return configured

    device_path = path or default_device_path()
    try:
        existing = device_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        existing = ""

    if existing:
        return existing

    device_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    device_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    device_path.write_text(device_id + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    return device_id
